policy: Original course and lesson indexes unchanged. Browser-local supplement progress; never claim Firebase sync or independent accreditation.

units.title: Linux files, permissions & evidence
units.subtitle: WSL 1 on a low-memory laptop
units.scenario: A learner needs to preserve a small training file and show its permissions before and after a safe change.

sections.heading: Inspect the current directory and its entries
sections.instruction: pwd reports the working directory; ls -la lists hidden files, modes, ownership, and sizes. Use this before making changes to avoid editing the wrong place.
sections.interpretation: A normal result begins with /home/<user> after cd ~. If it begins /mnt/c, you are working on the Windows filesystem; move back to your Linux home.
sections.task: In Ubuntu run: cd ~; mkdir -p ethical-hacking-labs; cd ethical-hacking-labs; pwd; ls -la. Record the returned path.
sections.safety: Only inspect and modify files you own. Linux permissions in WSL 1 do not create a security boundary against Windows.

sections.heading: Create and document a known test artifact
sections.instruction: printf emits controlled text; > replaces the destination file content. stat reports mode, owner, size and timestamps. Never redirect to an unknown important file.
sections.interpretation: The new file should have a size near 14 bytes; timestamps should reflect creation. The mode may depend on umask.
sections.task: Create evidence.txt in your training folder, run stat, and write down size, owner and current permissions.
sections.safety: Redirection overwrites files; use a disposable filename in your own lab.

sections.command: chmod 600 evidence.txt; ls -l evidence.txt; cat evidence.txt
sections.heading: Apply least privilege and verify read access
sections.instruction: chmod 600 grants read/write to the owner, nothing to group or others. ls verifies mode; cat checks the file remains readable by the owner.
sections.interpretation: The ls output should start -rw-------. If chmod fails, inspect file ownership and location.
sections.task: Explain why 600 is appropriate for a personal secret and why 644 would reveal data to other local users.
sections.safety: Avoid running chmod recursively or using 777 to bypass access problems.

units.title: Linux text processing & investigation notes
units.subtitle: Read-only evidence handling
units.scenario: A synthetic system log contains one failed sign-in among normal status messages.

sections.command: printf '%s\n' 'INFO boot ok' 'WARN failed login for guest' 'INFO backup ok' > auth-training.log
sections.heading: Create controlled log evidence
sections.instruction: printf produces predictable entries; a synthetic log removes the need to inspect real users' activity. Each entry conveys event type and message.
sections.interpretation: File should contain three lines. It does not prove real unauthorized access.
sections.task: Create the log in your training folder and explain the difference between WARN and confirmed compromise.
sections.safety: No real authentication logs or third-party user data are needed.

sections.heading: Find relevant events without discarding context
sections.instruction: grep -n finds matching lines with line numbers, while wc -l counts records. A narrow search can miss related events.
sections.interpretation: Expected: a WARN on line 2, and 3 total lines. No match results in grep exit status 1; that is not necessarily a crash.
sections.task: Identify the warning and state two additional facts you would need before attributing it to an attacker.
sections.safety: This is analysis of your own fictional file, not a live security alert.

sections.command: cp auth-training.log auth-copy.log; sha256sum auth-training.log auth-copy.log
sections.heading: Preserve and compare evidence
sections.instruction: cp creates a working copy. sha256sum calculates a cryptographic content digest; equal digests are strong evidence of identical file contents, not identity or time of acquisition.
sections.interpretation: Two equal 64-character hashes should appear. If they differ, investigate accidental edits rather than assume malicious tampering.
sections.task: Record both hashes, then explain why an evidence log needs timestamps and an acquisition narrative in addition to a hash.
sections.safety: Hash equality alone does not establish chain of custody.

units.title: Hardware diagnosis & component isolation
units.subtitle: Low-spec laptop repair scenario
units.scenario: A Windows laptop is slow and its memory graph shows limited free RAM.

sections.heading: Observe memory pressure
sections.instruction: Total capacity, in-use memory, commit, speed, and slots used are separate signals. High utilization alone does not prove failing hardware.
sections.interpretation: A 4 GB system with 2.6 GB in use has limited headroom; a 1-of-1 SODIMM entry suggests a single installed module but doesn't certify upgrade support.
sections.task: Write down observed RAM, usable capacity and available memory. Identify whether upgradeability requires a service-manual check.
sections.safety: Avoid purchasing replacement memory until exact model and supported module are confirmed.

sections.heading: Correlate workload with utilization
sections.instruction: Sort memory consumption to identify resource-heavy applications; include startup, background services and browser tab count.
sections.interpretation: Memory use by Windows can be normal. An application consuming more RAM than expected is a lead, not proof of malware.
sections.task: Compare memory usage with browser closed versus open. Report processes without disclosing personal app or account data.
sections.safety: Do not disable Windows security services to free RAM.

sections.heading: Assess the full system before recommending hardware
sections.instruction: Small eMMC drives can constrain Windows updates and swap. Storage space, RAM and CPU must be assessed together.
sections.interpretation: A system with limited free storage may slow down during updates; a RAM upgrade will not change CPU capability or drive capacity.
sections.task: Create a repair recommendation with evidence, the cheapest mitigation, and the limitations of upgrading.
sections.safety: Back up files before any hardware service.

units.title: PC assembly safety & fault trees
units.subtitle: POST failure on a training workstation
units.scenario: A machine powers on but produces intermittent memory test errors.

sections.heading: Define the failure boundary
sections.instruction: Separate no-power, no-POST, no-display and operating-system boot failure. These are different diagnostic branches.
sections.interpretation: A spinning fan does not establish a completed POST; an external display may help distinguish panel from system faults.
sections.task: Write a fault tree with at least three possible causes and a read-only observation for each.
sections.safety: Shut down, disconnect power, observe battery/ESD precautions before touching components.

sections.command: Read firmware memory inventory and test report
sections.heading: Triangulate independent evidence
sections.instruction: A repeated memory fault can involve a module, seating, a socket or timings. Compare slot and module behavior before concluding a part failed.
sections.interpretation: If errors follow the module to another approved slot, suspect module; if faults remain in one slot, suspect the board.
sections.task: Explain a controlled one-variable-at-a-time isolation test and the evidence each outcome would provide.
sections.safety: Never hot-swap memory or open a device with internal battery connected.

sections.heading: Close the ticket with proof
sections.instruction: A good service record includes preconditions, approvals, action, serial or asset information, post-change tests, and rollback.
sections.interpretation: A successful reboot after a replacement is only one piece of validation; run a repeat memory test.
sections.task: Draft a short service report and classify observed facts versus hypotheses.
sections.safety: Only use authorized equipment and protect customer data.

units.title: Networking: addressing, routes & DNS
units.subtitle: Isolated lab network reasoning
units.scenario: A workstation cannot load app.lab.example, yet the service responds by IP.

sections.heading: Establish local address and route
sections.instruction: ip -br addr shows interface address/state, and ip route shows the routing decision. Under WSL 1, networking inherits important Windows characteristics.
sections.interpretation: An address without a route to a remote subnet won't establish end-to-end reachability. A default route on WSL is normal: don't delete it for this lesson.
sections.task: Write down interfaces, private addresses and routes; classify each as local host, gateway or destination.
sections.safety: Do not change your real home router or WSL routes for this observation.

sections.heading: Check name-resolution output
sections.instruction: getent queries system name services and is useful for understanding resolver behavior. It doesn't show every DNS hop or prove an application works.
sections.interpretation: A result maps a name to an address; empty output could be name-resolution failure or unavailable internet.
sections.task: Explain what you'd investigate if names fail but addresses work, and why you should compare the expected IP.
sections.safety: Use public domains only for benign resolution, not scanning.

sections.heading: Calculate subnet size
sections.instruction: The ipaddress standard-library module avoids mental arithmetic mistakes when reading CIDR masks. A /24 includes 256 addresses total, with conventional network/broadcast reservations for IPv4 LANs.
sections.interpretation: Expected output is 256, not the number of simultaneously available hosts.
sections.task: Calculate usable hosts under conventional IPv4 addressing and explain why a /30 is different.
sections.safety: This calculation is offline and safe.

units.title: Linux accounts, processes & troubleshooting
units.subtitle: A fictional service appears to be down
units.scenario: A training operator sees an application failure and must collect observations without guessing.

sections.heading: Establish identity and group privileges
sections.instruction: whoami shows effective username, id reports UID and groups, groups lists memberships. Access control decisions depend on more than usernames.
sections.interpretation: If commands show the hp account and group, you're working as a normal user. Do not assume root rights.
sections.task: Explain the difference between ordinary user and root, and why least privilege reduces impact.
sections.safety: Avoid using sudo unless a lab exercise clearly requires it.

sections.heading: Inspect process context
sections.instruction: ps lists processes; piping to head limits output. Presence of a process doesn't prove that it is healthy or reachable.
sections.interpretation: WSL 1 process listings differ from a complete Ubuntu server; a service may not use systemd.
sections.task: Describe two checks beyond process presence needed to confirm a web application is working.
sections.safety: No service changes are required in this observation.

sections.command: printf '%s\n' 'ERROR backend timeout' 'INFO restart approved' > service-training.log; grep -n 'ERROR' service-training.log
sections.heading: Separate symptoms from cause
sections.instruction: A timeout is a symptom that can result from routing, DNS, application latency or dependency failures. A single log is not conclusive.
sections.interpretation: Expected: one ERROR line. An approval record is not a substitute for before/after service metrics.
sections.task: List at least three hypotheses and evidence that would discriminate among them.
sections.safety: Work from fictional logs and avoid touching real running services.

units.title: SOC triage: authentication and event correlation
units.subtitle: Change-window identity alert
units.scenario: A monitoring tool flags a sign-in during an approved deployment.

sections.command: Review timestamp, actor, device and outcome
sections.heading: Establish a factual timeline
sections.instruction: Each log source has its own clock and schema. Normalize time zones before interpreting event order. A sign-in alert alone does not prove compromise.
sections.interpretation: A sign-in at 09:12 within a 09:00–09:20 change window establishes overlap, not authorization for that individual login.
sections.task: Write an evidence table with fact, source, interpretation and uncertainty.
sections.safety: Use synthetic identities and preserve original records.

sections.command: Compare sign-in, change ticket and workload logs
sections.heading: Correlate independent sources
sections.instruction: A valid ticket and workload execution may support a benign hypothesis, but token issuer and device ownership can remain unknown.
sections.interpretation: Concordant timestamps increase confidence; missing device ownership must remain an open question.
sections.task: State which facts support benign and malicious hypotheses. Identify minimum extra evidence.
sections.safety: Do not claim an alert is false positive without sufficient corroboration.

sections.heading: Separate confidence from severity
sections.instruction: Disposition should include scope, known impact, residual risk, owner, deadline and rationale for escalation or closure.
sections.interpretation: A medium-confidence anomaly may warrant monitoring and verification without emergency intervention.
sections.task: Draft an escalation note and one follow-up control to reduce repeated alerts.
sections.safety: Never contact or access third-party systems as part of a fictional exercise.

units.title: Defensive cryptography & log integrity
units.subtitle: Evidence chain for local files
units.scenario: A practice log was copied for later review and must be verified as unchanged.

sections.heading: Hash a training artifact
sections.instruction: SHA-256 creates a fixed-length digest of contents. Identical digests strongly support content equality but can't prove authorship.
sections.interpretation: The hexadecimal hash is 64 characters; changing one character in the source should generally change the digest.
sections.task: Record the digest alongside the file path, acquisition timestamp, operator, and hash-tool version. Explain why matching digest values cannot establish who produced the original data or when.
sections.safety: Do not alter real evidence to test hash differences.

sections.heading: Compare an evidence copy
sections.instruction: An independent comparison helps detect corruption or modification between acquisition and review.
sections.interpretation: A matching digest on copied file demonstrates matching bytes, not proof of the original source's authenticity.
sections.task: Explain why digital signatures or trusted timestamps might be needed to establish provenance.
sections.safety: Perform all changes within your disposable training directory.

sections.heading: Choose appropriate controls
sections.instruction: Hashing checks integrity, encryption protects confidentiality, and digital signatures can support origin authentication and integrity under key-management assumptions.
sections.interpretation: Encrypted data can still be tampered with unless authenticated encryption or an appropriate MAC is used.
sections.task: Choose a security control for password storage, confidential transfer, and release provenance, with one reason each.
sections.safety: Never store actual passwords in your practice files.

units.title: Authorized web testing & server-side access
units.subtitle: Synthetic object-level authorization bug
units.scenario: A guest requests an account record that should belong only to an owner.

sections.command: Write scope and expected access matrix
sections.heading: Define before touching the application
sections.instruction: Authentication answers who claims to be present; authorization decides what resources that identity may access. An ethical assessment begins with written permission and boundaries.
sections.interpretation: A guest receiving HTTP 403 for private record is the expected result; HTTP 200 with private data is a possible defect.
sections.task: Build a role-to-object matrix with guest, owner and admin for one fictional private record.
sections.safety: Only run tests against Academy-owned synthetic targets.

sections.command: Compare predefined guest and owner responses
sections.heading: Use a controlled negative test
sections.instruction: A paired test uses the same object with distinct roles to isolate the permission decision. A UI-only restriction is not enough.
sections.interpretation: Guest 200 and owner 200 is suspicious if the guest isn't authorized; guest 403 and owner 200 is the expected protected behavior.
sections.task: Document method, request, status, returned fields, business impact and any ambiguity.
sections.safety: Do not try object IDs on a real website without explicit authorization.

sections.heading: Avoid false confidence after a patch
sections.instruction: A successful negative test must be accompanied by a positive test to ensure legitimate access remains available.
sections.interpretation: Denying all roles may stop disclosure but breaks the service, and should not receive full credit.
sections.task: Write two regression checks, one deny and one allow, and describe how to record them.
sections.safety: The Academy training server uses fictional role selectors, not production login controls.

units.title: Defensive Python automation & input safety
units.subtitle: Automate checks without creating new risk
units.scenario: A junior analyst needs to examine approved files and report mismatches.

sections.heading: Check the runtime and compatibility
sections.instruction: Different Python versions affect syntax and dependency availability. Record version before running scripts.
sections.interpretation: A modern Python 3 version is expected. If command is missing, check package availability rather than downloading random binaries.
sections.task: Record the exact Python version shown on your authorized Linux installation, then describe two compatibility risks, such as removed syntax or missing standard-library features, before running any script.
sections.safety: Use Python's standard library first on a low-memory laptop.

sections.heading: Read the current folder safely
sections.instruction: pathlib allows path manipulation without shell string concatenation. Inspect rather than modifying unknown paths.
sections.interpretation: Expected: your current Linux folder path. A path is data, not automatically a trusted location.
sections.task: Explain what could go wrong if a program accepts arbitrary relative paths.
sections.safety: Never construct shell commands by concatenating untrusted file names.

sections.heading: Understand deterministic hashes
sections.instruction: The same input bytes produce the same digest across runs. Use a known fixed string for repeatable practice.
sections.interpretation: A 64-character hex string is expected and should be identical on every run.
sections.task: Describe a scripted integrity check for your own lab file and what it does not prove.
sections.safety: Hashes are not passwords and this fixed example is not a secure secret.

units.title: Virtualization, WSL and training isolation
units.subtitle: Design a realistic low-resource lab
units.scenario: A 4 GB laptop cannot comfortably host two full Ubuntu virtual machines and Windows.

sections.heading: Identify the Linux execution model
sections.instruction: WSL 1 translates Linux system calls; WSL 2 uses a lightweight VM. They differ in compatibility, networking and resource requirements.
sections.interpretation: A VERSION 1 listing confirms the distribution uses WSL 1, not an isolated vulnerable target machine.
sections.task: Explain which lessons are appropriate on WSL 1 and which require a properly isolated VM.
sections.safety: Don't run intentionally vulnerable network servers on WSL connected to your home network.

sections.command: Plan CPU, RAM, storage and isolation
sections.heading: Compare resource constraints
sections.instruction: For a lab host, add guest RAM, host overhead and hypervisor overhead before scheduling workloads. Full VMs need dedicated storage.
sections.interpretation: Two 2 GB VMs plus Windows exceed practical headroom on a 4 GB laptop. This is a capacity limit, not a learner failure.
sections.task: Prepare a minimum/target specification for future lab hardware and an interim WSL curriculum.
sections.safety: Use low-memory local file exercises until upgraded hardware is available.

sections.command: Check virtual NIC types before launching targets
sections.heading: Know isolation modes
sections.instruction: Internal networks can isolate guests from the host/LAN; host-only often allows host connections; bridged exposes guests to the physical network.
sections.interpretation: An internal switch without a default route is preferable for intentionally vulnerable targets, but does not guarantee no compromise path.
sections.task: Write an isolation checklist with NIC types, gateway, host firewall, guest services and shutdown.
sections.safety: Never publish vulnerable training targets on GitHub Pages or forward their ports.

units.title: Cloud infrastructure trust boundaries
units.subtitle: Configuration review without cloud bills
units.scenario: A fictional organization exposes a private storage bucket through a mistaken policy.

sections.command: Define resource, principal, action and condition
sections.heading: Read identity-based policy semantics
sections.instruction: A cloud IAM rule combines what can be accessed, by whom, which actions are allowed, and contextual conditions. Least privilege reduces unnecessary blast radius.
sections.interpretation: Allowing all principals to read all objects is broad exposure; an explicit deny may take precedence depending on provider policy evaluation.
sections.task: Draft a least-privilege allow statement in plain English and state any expected policy precedence.
sections.safety: Do not deploy or alter real cloud services for this exercise.

sections.heading: Evaluate impact and detection
sections.instruction: An exposed policy is a configuration finding; actual data access requires separate access logs or other evidence.
sections.interpretation: A risk finding can exist even without evidence of an attacker accessing the object.
sections.task: Distinguish exposure from exploitation, and propose a monitoring query.
sections.safety: Synthetic examples avoid requiring paid cloud accounts.

sections.heading: Prevent recurrence
sections.instruction: Correct policy, verify authorized and unauthorized access, add preventive policy checks, and preserve rollback evidence.
sections.interpretation: A policy change without a deny/allow regression check has incomplete validation.
sections.task: Write a repair playbook: approve, snapshot policy, fix, test, monitor, rollback.
sections.safety: Cloud examples are conceptual until practiced in a controlled tenant.

units.title: Advanced detection: metrics and rule tuning
units.subtitle: SOC alert fatigue case
units.scenario: A detection fired on 24 events, 9 true incidents, and missed 6 other incidents.

sections.heading: Separate the four outcomes
sections.instruction: TP, FP, FN and TN quantify distinct performance dimensions; a rule can be precise while missing important events.
sections.interpretation: For 100 labeled examples, TP=9, FP=15, FN=6 and TN=70. The rule detected only 9 of 15 actual incidents, despite 79% overall accuracy; the denominator matters.
sections.task: Reconcile all four counts and explain the danger of looking only at total accuracy.
sections.safety: Use fictional labeled data and protect customer telemetry.

sections.heading: Evaluate detection trade-offs
sections.instruction: Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN). Tuning to reduce false positives may increase false negatives.
sections.interpretation: Precision = 9/(9+15) = 37.5% of issued alerts were truly positive. Recall = 9/(9+6) = 60% of actual incidents were detected; six incidents were missed.
sections.task: Calculate both values and propose a minimum-recall rule acceptance threshold.
sections.safety: No metric alone certifies detection quality.

sections.heading: Validate proposed production changes
sections.instruction: Tune with a training set, test on separately labeled holdout data, and monitor after deploy. Approval and rollback thresholds are required.
sections.interpretation: A rule suppressing all alerts has zero useful recall, even if false positives disappear.
sections.task: Specify a holdout dataset, minimum acceptable recall, maximum false-positive burden, owner approval, monitoring duration, and rollback trigger. State the baseline metrics used for comparison.
sections.safety: Do not disable production protections as part of a class exercise.

units.title: Professional scope, legal authorization & evidence
units.subtitle: Client assessment governance
units.scenario: A consultant receives an ambiguous request to assess a corporate web application.

sections.command: Define permission and assets in writing
sections.heading: Require explicit authorization
sections.instruction: Scope should list legal entity, authorized systems, dates, contact, technical limits and reporting channel. An informal message from an unknown requester is insufficient.
sections.interpretation: A hostname alone doesn't establish who owns the service or who is empowered to approve a test.
sections.task: Draft a written authorization checklist naming the legal owner and verified signer, included and excluded assets, permitted methods, dates, emergency contact, and conditions requiring immediate termination.
sections.safety: Do not perform live testing until owner authorization is verified.

sections.command: Create safe test plan and stop conditions
sections.heading: Reduce avoidable disruption
sections.instruction: Use known low-impact tests first. Declare rate limits, prohibited techniques, emergency contacts and stop conditions.
sections.interpretation: Unusual 5xx error spikes or unexpected sensitive data may trigger a stop-and-escalate decision.
sections.task: Draft a two-stage discovery-and-validation plan and identify evidence needed at each stage.
sections.safety: Never reuse real exposed data as a demonstration artifact.

sections.heading: Explain findings responsibly
sections.instruction: A report should include affected asset, evidence, exploit prerequisites, realistic impact, likelihood, limitations, fix and retest.
sections.interpretation: A medium-severity hypothetical does not automatically establish business-critical compromise.
sections.task: Write executive and technical summaries of the same fictional issue.
sections.safety: Avoid claiming certification or external audit approval from self-authored work.

units.title: Capstone: multi-cause incident reconstruction
units.subtitle: Complex outage with concurrent faults
units.scenario: A fictional enterprise suffers DNS resolver errors and application queue saturation in the same hour.

sections.heading: Avoid single-cause assumptions
sections.instruction: Correlate alerts by timestamp and data source. Two symptoms can share an origin or be independent.
sections.interpretation: 09:14 resolver alarm and 09:16 HTTP 503 spike do not prove one caused the other.
sections.task: Create a timeline with fact/source/confidence columns; list two competing causal models.
sections.safety: Operate only on supplied synthetic records.

sections.heading: Demand independent observables
sections.instruction: DNS lookup, TCP connection, HTTP status and business transaction are different layers; each can recover while another remains impaired.
sections.interpretation: DNS errors falling to 0.5% doesn't prove queue length normalized; service still may fail.
sections.task: Specify pre/post checks for resolver error rate, 503 rate, queue depth and a known-good transaction.
sections.safety: Do not change production network routing as a shortcut.

sections.heading: Use controlled change management
sections.instruction: Containment, approval, reversible remediation, success criteria and long-term prevention should be documented separately.
sections.interpretation: A successful rollback of one fault with continuing service errors must be reported as partial recovery.
sections.task: Write an incident report and state which evidence would be necessary for sign-off.
sections.safety: Real system sign-off requires trained operators and independent review.

units.title: Capstone: independent security assessment report
units.subtitle: Board-level and technical communication
units.scenario: Present a synthetic security assessment covering access controls, identity and monitoring.

sections.heading: Separate observed fact from opinion
sections.instruction: A report must identify what was tested, what was not, sources, permission, timing and any constraints on conclusions.
sections.interpretation: A simulated HTTP 200 response demonstrates the scenario behavior but does not prove actual compromise.
sections.task: Write a scope declaration and evidence inventory for three fictional issues.
sections.safety: Don't imply independent accreditation or penetration-testing certification.

sections.heading: Relate security issues to business risk
sections.instruction: Risk severity depends on exposure, exploit conditions, asset sensitivity, controls and likelihood—not CVSS alone.
sections.interpretation: An unauthenticated private-report exposure may be urgent; an internal-only diagnostic warning can be lower risk depending on impact.
sections.task: Prepare a triage table with severity, confidence, owner, deadline and retest criteria.
sections.safety: Be careful not to include secrets in a report.

sections.heading: Explain trade-offs under questioning
sections.instruction: An assessor should challenge assumptions, false positives, available evidence, residual risk, rollback and cost.
sections.interpretation: High confidence requires corroboration, not merely long narratives or a 100-point automated score.
sections.task: Write an executive summary of 200 words and a separate technical appendix, then list five reviewer questions.
sections.safety: A self-graded portfolio is not equivalent to professional licensure.
